Issued at 259 AM EDT Thu Oct 29 2026

Today through Saturday...

Mostly clear skies are observed on nighttime microphysics satellite 
imagery early this morning, with an area of mid-level clouds noted 
just to the northwest of the area. These clouds are associated with 
very modest moisture transport ahead of a sfc cold front currently 
analyzed over the upper Midwest. Over the next 24 hours, this cold 
front will gradually work its way toward the area, although it is 
expected to fall apart as it makes its way into the lower Ohio 
Valley late tonight into Friday morning.

Today, ahead of the front, 5-10 mph SW breezes should pick up by the 
late morning hours, continuing through late afternoon. This 
combination of warm advection with mostly sunny skies today should 
allow temperatures to reach 1-2 degrees above persistence, with 
forecast highs ranging from 75-80.

This evening into tonight, the front will begin to make its way into 
southern IN, likely bringing a broken band of low-mid level clouds 
with it. While there is a 5% chance of a spotty shower in southern 
IN, moisture will be lacking and no impacts are expected. These 
clouds will keep temperatures milder along and north of I-64 
tonight, with the typical ridge-valley splits being much more 
pronounced across southern KY where skies should remain mostly clear.

Friday, what's left of the front is expected to settle near the 
KY/TN border, with winds shifting around to the NE in its wake as 
high pressure moves across the lower Great Lakes. This should bring 
marginally cooler temperatures across the northern half of the CWA 
Friday afternoon, with highs ranging from the mid 70s in the north 
to near 80 in southern KY.

Friday night into Saturday, a mid-level vort max associated with the 
remnants of TC Vance is expected to lift out of the southern Plains 
and into the mid-Miss. Valley. This disturbance will allow mid- and 
upper-level moisture to advect in from the SW, with clouds 
increasing during this period. Models are now in relatively good 
agreement that Saturday will remain dry across the area, as a fairly 
large amount of dry air below 700 mb will have to be overcome by 
modest moisture advection. With the increased cloud cover, 
temperatures should be slightly milder Friday night, with highs 
slightly less warm Saturday afternoon (though still above normal). 

Saturday Night through Monday Night...

The disturbance referenced above is expected to slowly move across 
the Ohio Valley Saturday night into Sunday, weakening as large-scale 
ridging develops across the central CONUS. There is still a fair 
amount of disagreement among model families only 3-4 days out, 
though there is increasing confidence that the impacts from this 
system will be minimal. The ECMWF and CMC ensembles tend toward an 
overall weaker system, with less moisture advection (only 1-1.2" 
PWATs) and very isolated showers and most locations remaining dry. 
On the other hand, the GFS and its ensembles have a stronger 
shortwave and richer moisture advection (1.3-1.4" PWATs), with much 
more widespread rain on Sunday. At this time, we're looking at 
roughly coin flip odds for rain this weekend, though there is high 
(80%) confidence that rainfall amounts will be less than 0.50".

With mostly cloudy skies and limiting nighttime cooling and daytime 
heating, diurnal ranges in temperatures will be suppressed for the 
second half of the weekend into Monday, though both highs and low 
temperatures will be above normal. Residual moisture may lead to 
isolated showers on Monday; however, precipitation coverage is 
expected to be limited by weak forcing.

Middle of Next Week...

A much more dynamic pattern returns by the middle of next week, 
bringing chances for rain, possibly thunderstorms, as well as the 
potential for fluctuating temperatures. A coupled polar and 
subtropical stream trough over the Pacific NW this weekend is 
expected to come out of phase as it crosses the Rockies early next 
week, causing an overall slowdown in the system. At this point, 
ensemble 500 mb height cluster analysis reveals several different 
camps of model solutions, resulting in different weather impacts to 
the area over the middle of next week. It is very likely that this 
disturbance will eject across the region some time in the Tuesday 
night-Thursday time period, bringing a wave of moisture as it passes 
along with cooler temperatures behind the system. Some of the 
stronger solutions could even bring a chance for strong storms into 
the area, as deep-layer shear would be seasonably strong. However, 
instability appears to be the main limiting factor, and AI/ML medium-
range severe convection guidance isn't overly concerning at this 
time. Regardless, we'll continue to monitor this time period over 
the next several days for the potential for impactful rainfall 
amounts and strong storms.
